concept.body: Read hierarchy claims by direction. UP the family tree (specific → general): always true — a square is always a rhombus. DOWN the tree (general → specific): sometimes true — a rhombus is a square only when right angles appear. ACROSS disjoint branches (parallelogram vs trapezoid under the exactly-one-pair convention): never.

explanationVariants: Rhombus → parallelogram travels UP the tree (a rhombus is a special parallelogram): always.
Every rhombus satisfies the parallelogram definition — up-flow is automatic.

options.label: Always true — up the tree
options.feedback: Rhombus is defined as a parallelogram with congruent sides; membership flows upward unconditionally.

options.label: Sometimes true
options.feedback: There's no condition attached — the parallelogram requirement is inside the rhombus definition. Always.

options.label: Never true
options.feedback: The rhombus region sits wholly INSIDE the parallelogram region — the claim can't fail.

options.label: True only for squares
options.feedback: Leaning rhombi qualify equally — all of them are parallelograms. Always.

steps.body: The family tree is a logic machine. **Always** true: any claim that flows UP the tree (a square is always a rhombus). **Sometimes**: claims that flow DOWN (a rhombus is sometimes a square — when right angles show up). **Never**: claims that jump between disjoint branches (under our convention, a parallelogram is never a trapezoid).

explanationVariants: Rectangles sit inside the parallelogram region — every rectangle inherits the definition. Always.
Up-the-tree claims are automatic: rectangle ⇒ parallelogram, always.

widget.prompt: “A rectangle is a parallelogram.” Always, sometimes, or never?

options.label: Always — rectangle is DEFINED as a special parallelogram
options.feedback: Membership flows up: every rectangle carries the parallelogram definition inside its own.

options.label: Sometimes — only when the sides differ
options.feedback: Side lengths never matter for this one — the parallelogram requirement is built into being a rectangle. Always.

options.label: Never — they're different shapes
options.feedback: Different NAMES, nested sets: the rectangle region lives wholly inside the parallelogram region.

options.label: Sometimes — only when it's also a square
options.feedback: Squarehood is irrelevant here; even the most elongated rectangle is a parallelogram. Always.

explanationVariants: Down-the-tree: a parallelogram is a rectangle only when a right angle appears — sometimes.
Some parallelograms lean (no), some stand square (yes): sometimes.

widget.prompt: “A parallelogram is a rectangle.” Always, sometimes, or never?

options.label: Sometimes — exactly when it has a right angle
options.feedback: Downward claims are conditional: the leaning ones fail, the right-angled ones qualify.

options.label: Always — the terms coincide
options.feedback: A 60°-leaning parallelogram is the counterexample — no right angles, no rectangle. Sometimes.

options.label: Never — parallelograms exclude rectangles
options.feedback: Rectangles are IN the parallelogram family — the claim succeeds precisely on those members. Sometimes.

options.label: Sometimes — exactly when all sides are congruent
options.feedback: All-congruent-sides makes a RHOMBUS. The rectangle condition is the right ANGLE. Sometimes, but for the angle reason.

steps.body: Two placements trip everyone. **A square is always a rhombus AND always a rectangle** — it sits at the intersection, holding both memberships fully. And under our EXACTLY-one-pair convention, **a parallelogram is never a trapezoid**: two parallel pairs is one too many for the trapezoid branch.

explanationVariants: Our convention demands EXACTLY one parallel pair — a parallelogram's two pairs disqualify it. Never.
The branches are disjoint by definition here (the “at least one” convention would answer differently).

widget.prompt: Under this course's convention, “a parallelogram is a trapezoid” is:

options.label: Never true — exactly one parallel pair excludes two-pair figures
options.feedback: The exclusive definition splits the branches cleanly: two parallel pairs means not-a-trapezoid, full stop.

options.label: Always true — it has at least one parallel pair
options.feedback: That's the OTHER convention (“at least one”). Ours says exactly one, so parallelograms are excluded.

options.label: Sometimes true — when it leans
options.feedback: Leaning never removes the second parallel pair — every parallelogram keeps both pairs at any slant. Never.

options.label: Sometimes true — when it's a rhombus
options.feedback: A rhombus has two parallel pairs like every parallelogram — still excluded under exactly-one. Never.

predict.prompt: You will place the corner so all four sides equal 5. Will that alone make it a square, or only a rhombus?

options.label: Only a rhombus — equal sides say nothing about the angles
A square — four equal sides is exactly what a square means
It depends where the other three corners were pinned

predict.reveal: Only a rhombus. Four equal sides leave the angles free to lean — "all sides equal" is ALWAYS true of a square but only SOMETIMES gives you one. That gap is the whole point of always/sometimes/never.

widget.prompt: Pinned at (0,0), (5,0) and (8,4). Place the fourth corner so every side is 5 — a rhombus.
widget.successFeedback: (3, 4): all four sides 5, but the diagonals are 8.94 and 4.47 — UNEQUAL. So this rhombus is not a rectangle, and certainly not a square. 'A rhombus is sometimes a rectangle' is now a claim you have tested rather than recited: it happens exactly when the diagonals agree.
widget.sideFeedback: Not in the right column: the sides cannot all reach 5 from there.
widget.angleFeedback: Right column, wrong height — check the four side lengths, which must all be 5.

cml.actionGoal: Move one vertex while side, diagonal, angle, and family evidence update together.

widget.prompt: “A rhombus is a kite.” Under the standard (inclusive) kite definition used in ch4, this is:

options.label: Always — four congruent sides qualify
options.feedback: A rhombus over-delivers on the kite's requirement: four congruent sides split into BOTH consecutive pairs congruent, each pair matching. That's why ½·d₁·d₂ covers rhombi.

options.label: Never — kites can't have parallel sides
options.feedback: The kite definition demands congruent consecutive pairs and says nothing forbidding parallels — rhombi qualify.

options.label: Sometimes — only for squares
options.feedback: EVERY rhombus qualifies, leaning or square: four equal sides always split into two congruent consecutive pairs.

options.label: Sometimes — only when the diagonals are equal
options.feedback: Diagonal lengths don't gate kite membership — the side pairs do, and a rhombus always has them.

hints: Claim A flows up the tree; claim B flows down; claim C jumps branches.
Up = always. Down = sometimes. Disjoint jump (our convention) = never.
A: square→rectangle. B: rectangle→square. C: rhombus→trapezoid.
explanationVariants: A square is always a rectangle (up); a rectangle is sometimes a square (down — needs equal sides); a rhombus is never a trapezoid (two parallel pairs, exclusive convention).
Always / sometimes / never, in that order — the tree's three directions.

widget.prompt: Verdicts for: (A) a square is a rectangle; (B) a rectangle is a square; (C) a rhombus is a trapezoid.

options.label: A: always. B: sometimes. C: never
options.feedback: Up-flow, down-flow, branch-jump — the three logical directions of the family tree, one of each.

options.label: A: sometimes. B: sometimes. C: sometimes
options.feedback: Only B is conditional. A holds by definition (up-flow); C is blocked by the exactly-one-pair convention.

options.label: A: always. B: never. C: never
options.feedback: B isn't never — rectangles with congruent consecutive sides ARE squares. Down-flow means sometimes.

options.label: A: always. B: sometimes. C: always
options.feedback: C fails our convention: a rhombus's TWO parallel pairs exceed the trapezoid's exactly-one. Never.

takeaways: Up the tree: always. Down the tree: sometimes. Across disjoint branches: never (exclusive convention).
The square holds dual citizenship: always a rectangle AND always a rhombus.
Regular quadrilateral = square: ch1's angle formula meets the hierarchy.
steps.teaser: Finale: mixed dispatch — read the markings, name the most specific shape, compute.
